old: "Couldn't he stop and take it all back... and not go?"
new: "Couldn't I stop and take it all back... and not go?"
reason: Inside his own quoted thought the switch to 'he' makes a listener wonder who else is meant; first person keeps the speaker clear.

old: turned off his path, and walked along it toward the Hay Market
new: turned off his path, and crossed it toward the Hay Market
reason: 'walked along it' leaves unclear whether 'it' is the bridge or the path and what he actually did; 'crossed it' makes the route clear.

A translator's footnote appears mid-scene as if it were narrative, and 'The translator's note read' sounds like an object in the story; it at least needs to be marked clearly as an editorial note (an editor may prefer to move it out of the reading text).

old: Before him stood the same peasant who had jostled past on the stairs.
new: Before him stood the same porter who had jostled past on the stairs.
reason: The previous paragraph says a porter pushed past him on the stairs, so 'the same peasant' sounds like a different person.

old: whom he had supported almost since he was thirteen
new: whom the student had supported almost since he was thirteen
reason: With Raskolnikov and the student both in the sentence, 'he' is ambiguous about who supported the father from age thirteen.

old: their mother overhearing her talk in her sleep
new: their mother overhearing Dounia talk in her sleep
reason: 'her' could be the mother or Dounia; naming Dounia shows who talked in her sleep.

old: he smiled strangely at his sister and Razumihin's passionate plans
new: he smiled strangely at the passionate plans of his sister and Razumihin
reason: Heard aloud, 'smiled strangely at his sister' first sounds complete, so the listener has to reparse the sentence.
'Burnous' is an obscure period garment; adding 'cloak' tells the listener what it is and keeps the word.
